section_summary: The section completes Stephen Naft's wartime propaganda study “Japan's Menace to the Americas,” covering state Shinto and Hakko Ichiu, Japanese social conditions, occupation policies in Korea, China, and Manchuria, alleged atrocities, and a lengthy bibliography. State Department correspondence then debates the study's suitability for radio propaganda, with reviewers warning that chapters III–V contain sensational or misleading generalizations. The final pages turn to the FBI's JAPSA investigation of a Japanese espionage and coded-correspondence network operating through commercial firms, lawyers, and intermediaries in Argentina, Brazil, and Chile.

subfiles.title: Japan's Menace to the Americas: Shinto, the “New Order,” conclusion, and bibliography
subfiles.to: Radio Division, Coordinator of Inter-American Affairs
subfiles.about: The concluding portion of a wartime study argues that Japanese religious ideology, domestic institutions, and occupation practices reveal an ambition for imperial world rule.
subfiles.summary: The study links State Shinto and Hakko Ichiu to claims of the Japanese emperor's divine and universal authority. It portrays Japanese workers, peasants, and women as oppressed by a military-financial oligarchy and presents Korea, China, and Manchuria as examples of the coercive “New Order,” including land seizure, narcotics, forced assimilation, and atrocities. After describing the Nanjing massacre and quoting threats against the United States, it closes with Joseph Grew's call to destroy Japanese militarism and a bibliography covering imperialism, Latin America, Shinto, and occupation policy.

subfiles.title: Letter transmitting “Japan's Menace to the Americas”
subfiles.to: John Begg, Assistant Chief, Division of Cultural Relations, Department of State
subfiles.about: Don Francisco submits Stephen Naft's study for State Department review, use, and comment.
subfiles.summary: Francisco describes the study as timely in anticipation of intensified Pacific operations. He identifies Naft as its author, credits Gabrielle Swados and Russell Pierce, and explains that the documented material was prepared for Western Hemisphere radio programming.

subfiles.title: Note forwarding two copies of the CIAA survey on Japan
subfiles.about: Yahraes forwards two copies of the Coordinator of Inter-American Affairs survey and asks for comments.
subfiles.summary: The note records that Mr. Dreier had already mentioned the survey to Myers. One copy was expected to be sent to the Division of Far Eastern Affairs, and Yahraes requested the division's comments.

subfiles.title: Title page: “Japan's Menace to the Americas”
subfiles.to: Radio Division, Coordinator of Inter-American Affairs
subfiles.about: The title leaf identifies the study, its author, commissioning office, and year.
subfiles.summary: The page gives the report's full title, “Japan's Menace to the Americas.” It states that Stephen Naft prepared it for the Radio Division of the Coordinator of Inter-American Affairs in 1943.

subfiles.title: Memorandum requesting detailed Far Eastern comments on the pamphlet
subfiles.from: Wells Stabler, Division of the American Republics
subfiles.to: Mr. Benninghoff, Division of Far Eastern Affairs
subfiles.about: Stabler requests detailed comments on objections to chapters III–V before Ecuadorian radio programs are based on the pamphlet.
subfiles.summary: Stabler forwards the Radio Division pamphlet following a telephone conversation with Benninghoff. He explains that the Coordination Committee in Ecuador plans radio programs based on it and that the Quito mission should receive the Department's comments.

subfiles.title: Draft instruction to the American Mission at Quito
subfiles.to: Officer in Charge, American Mission, Quito
subfiles.about: The draft transmits Don Francisco's communication concerning Ecuadorian radio scripts based on “Japan's Menace to the Americas.”
subfiles.summary: The instruction sends communication E-1537 of August 30, 1943, from Radio Division director Don Francisco to the Ecuador Coordination Committee. The mission is asked to forward it if there is no objection and to retain a copy, while observing specified precautions in preparing radio scripts.

subfiles.title: Comments on chapters III–VI of “Japan's Menace to the Americas”
subfiles.from: Division of Far Eastern Affairs reviewer
subfiles.to: Division of the American Republics and the Quito mission
subfiles.about: The reviewer identifies factual and propagandistic problems in the pamphlet's treatment of Shinto, Japanese society, women, and prostitution.
subfiles.summary: The comments accept much of chapter III but reject the broad claim that Japan intends to impose Shinto on all conquered peoples, suggesting instead that propaganda emphasize Japanese manipulation of the Catholic Church in the Philippines. Chapter IV is judged unfair and inaccurate concerning popular attitudes, women's legal status, and an alleged white-slave monopoly drawn from Alexander Pernikoff. The reviewer offers no particular suggestions on chapters V and VI and assumes the questionable material will not be quoted directly.

subfiles.title: Request for Far Eastern comments on the report
subfiles.from: John Begg, Division of Cultural Relations
subfiles.about: Begg asks Myers and his Far Eastern colleagues to review and comment on the report.
subfiles.summary: Begg states that he has read the report with interest. He requests any comments that Myers or other officers in Far Eastern Affairs wish to provide.

subfiles.title: Memorandum questioning chapters III–V of “Japan's Menace to the Americas”
subfiles.about: Myers advises against using chapters III–V as Latin American propaganda background without revision.
subfiles.summary: Myers acknowledges that much of the material can be substantiated but calls the chapters a compilation of sensational features lacking proper perspective. He warns that readers unfamiliar with Japan could receive a distorted impression and recommends appropriate revision before use.

subfiles.title: Confidential summary concerning Francisco Ortiz correspondence
subfiles.to: Department of State and other previous recipients
subfiles.about: The memorandum summarizes intercepted letters associated with Francisco Ortiz and Japanese-language or coded communications routed through Brazilian addressees.
subfiles.summary: The office's records concern passengers scheduled to arrive in Miami on November 23, 1943, particularly Francisco Ortiz. Letters to Alberto Góes Telles and Ary de Andrade Figueira contained Japanese enclosures, a coded message, and material addressed to R. Nagai. A decoded passage indicated that censorship had impeded communications addressed to Ortiz.

subfiles.title: FBI memorandum forwarding additional information on the JAPSA case
subfiles.to: Adolf A. Berle Jr., Assistant Secretary of State
subfiles.about: The FBI forwards an updated Rio de Janeiro summary and relationship chart concerning a Japanese espionage network in Argentina, Brazil, and Chile.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum describes five intercepted coded messages and identifies Suetaka Hayao, Francisco Ortiz, Rodolfo Ibarra, Alberto Veloz, and the Cándido Santidrián cover identity as important leads. It reports that Japanese subjects active in Chile had been repatriated and reviews Goro Miyasaki's espionage history and later movements with Hidenosuke Ueda in Argentina. Copies were supplied to Naval Intelligence and Army G-2, while investigation in Argentina and Brazil continued.

subfiles.title: JAPSA Case: Isoma Kobayashi–Francisco Ortiz
subfiles.from: Federal Bureau of Investigation, Rio de Janeiro investigation
subfiles.to: Adolf A. Berle Jr. and intelligence recipients
subfiles.about: The report reconstructs Japanese correspondence channels and commercial cover relationships centered on Isoma Kobayashi, Francisco Ortiz, Ryokichi Nagai, Alberto Góes Telles, and the Sociedade Comercial Nipo-Brasileira.
subfiles.summary: Investigators trace intercepted letters from the Nambei Trading Company in Buenos Aires through Ortiz and Brazilian lawyers to Nagai and former diplomat Suetaka Hayao, including coded or ciphered enclosures. The report examines Ary Figueira's and Alberto Góes Telles's representation of the Sociedade Comercial Nipo-Brasileira, Mitsui's effort to preserve “sleeper companies,” corporate personnel, strategic-material transactions, mail-box access, and suspected intelligence uses. It also profiles Telles and his daughter Lyzette, records their Japanese contacts and sympathies, and follows Telles's meetings with Japanese, Integralista, commercial, and precious-stones contacts in Rio. The attachment continues beyond page 450.
